input.body:
Fixes the duplicate-execution bug reported in #452 — and the duplicate work around it (#455, and the duplicate tracker issues / duplicate filings listed below).

## The bug

`run.mjs` files each dispatch issue **with its ready label already applied**, and one scheduler run files every due task's issue within a couple of seconds. So **one run emits one label event per issue and starts one executor session per event**.

`executor.md` step 1 then told every one of those sessions:

> Also list every *other* open issue carrying the same ready label … process them after it

So each of N sessions built the same N-issue work list. The step-3 claim swap was supposed to stop the overlap, but it could not: every session read the work list at startup, **before any claim landed**, and the swap was a blind label write with no compare-and-swap behind it. The guard only ever covered a race it was not in position to see.

## What it did on 2026-07-26

The 11:00 run filed #425–#430 in two seconds; five carried `ready-for-agent`.

- **#452** — dispatch #427 independently claimed, dispatched and converged by two sessions.
- **#425** (`conversation-extract`) ran at least three times: #435, #445, #446, #448 are four duplicate `Claudinite tracker: Conversation Extract` issues, created seconds apart by different subagents each doing find-by-title-else-create. It ended in `needs-human`.
- **#439, #449, #454** — three independent filings of the same dangling-links finding, with #439 and #440 as overlapping PRs. This is the "multiple routines make the same changes" symptom.

## The fix

**Executor — one session, one issue.**
- A session's work list is exactly the issue that triggered it. No sibling sweep, no backstop sweep. Concurrency between sessions stays normal and becomes safe by construction rather than by a claim taken too late to matter. A narrow fallback covers a session that genuinely cannot identify its trigger: take the single oldest armed issue, never more than one.
- The claim becomes a **verified lease**: read labels and abandon if already taken → swap and post a claim comment → re-read and yield to the earliest claim. GitHub has no compare-and-swap on labels; the confirm step is what makes the claim mean anything, and its absence is what let a duplicate through.

**Scheduler — recovery moves into code, in one place.** `maintainDispatchIssues` runs once per hourly run, over pure rules in `dispatch.mjs`:
1. **Stale** — dispatch open past ~2 of its own periods → comment, drop the ready label, `needs-human`. `staleDispatchIssues` was specified in the design and unit-tested, but **never actually wired into `main()`** — this connects it.
2. **Dead claim** — `agent-running` idle ~3h → comment, drop the claim, `needs-human`. Scoped to `[claudinite-task]` titles, so a task's claim on an issue *it* owns is never swept (this was the executor's old step 6, which every concurrent session ran in parallel).
3. **Re-arm** — armed, unclaimed, uncommented, past a 20-minute grace → the trigger event was lost, so remove and re-add its own ready label to emit a fresh one. Remove-then-add is load-bearing: re-applying a label already present emits no `labeled` event. A fleet dispatch re-arms under the fleet label, never the self one.

Stale wins over re-arm, so an issue converging to triage is never put back into circulation — and stale is what bounds the re-arm loop when the executor is down for good.

## Testing

690 tests pass; conformance sweep is 0 blocking (6 pre-existing advisories).

New tests cover each rule and the shell's actual GitHub calls — the label sequencing, ensure-before-apply ordering, and that an idle repo writes nothing. Per the repo's see-it-fail discipline they were checked against real mutations, not just run green: dropping the stale-exclusion from the re-arm set and collapsing remove-then-add into a bare re-apply each fail tests (3 failures across both changes).

## Note

`executor.md` is in the vendored engine set, so consuming repos pick this up through their next baselining.

One thing I could not check from here: whether more than one CCR routine is registered against `ready-for-agent`. If two are wired to the same label, every dispatch starts two sessions regardless of this change — worth confirming in the routine list. The verified claim lease means they would now collide harmlessly rather than duplicating work, but the wasted sessions would be real.

Done — [PR #461](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/461).

## What was wrong

Two defects that compounded, and neither could be fixed alone:

**Fan-out.** `run.mjs` files each dispatch issue with its ready label already attached, and one scheduler run files every due task's issue within seconds. One run → one label event per issue → **one session per event**. Today's 11:00 run filed #425–#430 and started five.

**No mutual exclusion.** `executor.md` then told every one of those five sessions to also drain its siblings, so each built the same 5-issue work list. The claim swap was meant to prevent overlap but couldn't — every session read the list *before* any claim landed, and the swap was a blind write with no compare-and-swap behind it. The guard covered a race it was never in position to see.

That's why you saw the same changes made repeatedly: #427 ran twice, #425 ran three times leaving four duplicate tracker issues, and the same dangling-links finding was filed three times (#439, #449, #454) with two overlapping PRs.

## What changed

- **One session runs exactly one issue** — the one that triggered it. Concurrency becomes safe by construction instead of by a claim taken too late.
- **The claim is now a verified lease** — read, swap + claim comment, then re-read and yield to the earliest claim. GitHub has no CAS on labels; the confirm step is what the old blind swap was missing.
- **Recovery moved into scheduler code**, in one place, running once per hour: stale escalation, dead-claim reclaim, and re-arming a lost trigger event. Two things worth flagging there — `staleDispatchIssues` was specified and unit-tested but **never wired into `main()`**, so that backstop has been dead code all along; and the executor's old step-6 stale-claim sweep had the same duplicate-work defect in miniature, so it moved too.

690 tests pass, conformance sweep clean. The new tests were verified against mutations rather than just run green — dropping the stale-exclusion and collapsing remove-then-add each fail tests.

Two things I did not resolve:

- I skipped the routine-registry check you interrupted. If more than one CCR routine is wired to `ready-for-agent`, every dispatch starts two sessions regardless of this fix. The verified lease means they'd now collide harmlessly rather than duplicate work, but the wasted sessions would be real — worth a look at your routine list.
- #455 (auto-merge unusable on this repo) is a genuine separate problem this doesn't touch; it needs the repo setting enabled.

Want me to watch #461 and handle CI failures or review comments as they come in?

> ⚠️ **Still open:** confirm no duplicate routine is registered against `ready-for-agent`; #455 needs the "Allow auto-merge" repo setting.

---
name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---


The portable recipe for landing the change in front of the owner on `main` — the *mechanics* behind the owner's merge-to-main command (the owner's preferences own the trigger *phrase*; this file owns the *how*). Invoked through the `merge-to-main` skill (this skill); this doc stays the canonical recipe.

**A project's bespoke merge policy overrides this default.** Most projects need nothing here — this default is the whole story. A project that genuinely diverges (a different merge method, a CI/twice-green gate, an extra approval) **states so by naming its merge-policy file explicitly in its own `CLAUDE.md`**. When that declaration is present, read that file first and let it override the divergent points below; when it's absent, follow this default as-is. Don't go hunting for a policy file that the project's `CLAUDE.md` doesn't name.

## Recipe (~4 calls)

1. Load both GitHub tools in **one** `ToolSearch`: `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request`.
2. No PR open for the branch yet? `create_pull_request` (base `main`); end the body with `Closes #<issue>`, and take the PR number from the returned URL.
3. Gate on CI **only if the repo has it** — a workflow that actually runs on PRs/pushes. `workflow_call`-only reusable workflows (this repo hosts some) are *not* CI: they never run here, so a non-empty `.github/workflows/` alone proves nothing; check the PR for check runs instead. No CI → no gate; don't wait for checks that will never come.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Merge directly — don't pre-read status; the call fails loudly if it isn't mergeable.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.

The two divergent points — **`squash`** as the method and **CI gating** — are exactly what a bespoke policy file changes.

## After the merge: capture the conversation (every session, every user)

Once the merge has landed and local `main` is synced, run the growth pack's capture step:
`node .claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>` (from the canon repo itself: `node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), `<n>` being the issue your `Closes #<issue>` named. Deterministic, seconds-long; it pushes the conversation to the orphan `conversation-logs` branch. It runs **here, in-session, because it needs the live transcript** — the lessons extraction then happens later in the fleet's `conversation-extract` run_daily task (central, MCP-native, with a rethink window), so there is nothing to schedule and no in-session lessons pass ([the pack README](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/README.md) owns the standard). A later merge in the same session just runs capture again — it captures the delta. In the rare repo that removed the `grow_with_claudinite` pack from `.claudinite-checks.json`, skip this step.

## Don't

- **Don't** re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge; trust it.

input.commit_message:
One scheduler run files every due task's dispatch issue seconds apart, each
already labeled, so one run started one executor session per issue — and
executor.md then told each session to also drain its siblings. The claim swap
could not prevent the resulting race: every session read the work list before
any of them claimed, and the swap was a blind write with no compare-and-swap.

Executor now runs exactly the one issue that triggered it, and its claim is a
verified lease (read, swap + claim comment, re-read and yield to the earliest).
Recovery — stale escalation, dead-claim reclaim, and re-arming a lost trigger
event — moves into scheduler code running once per hourly run. This also wires
staleDispatchIssues into main(), where it had been specified and tested but
never actually called.

Closes #452
